title: Gentle words for an angry guest
hookLine: Shishupala makes his case against Krishna's honor, and Yudhishthira goes after him with gentle words
carry: true, kind, helpful speech is a tapas
last: THE FIRST OFFERING GOES TO GOD.

lines: NOT THE ELDEST, NOT THE TEACHER.
cards: Shishupala has the floor, and he isn't shouting nonsense. That's what makes this scene uncomfortable. He's built an argument, point by point, and he delivers it to a hall full of kings.
If you wanted to honor age, there are elders here. If you wanted to honor a teacher, there's a teacher here. If you wanted to honor a king, Krishna isn't even a crowned king.
So why him? It's the kind of speech that makes a room shift in its seats.

teach.b: In the telling, Shishupala goes through the room like a lawyer. He names the honored elders sitting right there: the great teacher Drona, the sage Vyasa, Bhishma himself. Any of them, he says, had a better claim.

Then the argument turns into insult. The Pandavas have shamed themselves, he says, and Krishna has shamed himself by accepting what wasn't his. With that he gets up to leave, and some of the kings stir with him.
Now watch Yudhishthira. It's his great day, and his choice has just been mocked. He doesn't send a guard or trade insults.
He goes after Shishupala himself and speaks gently: this isn't a fitting way to speak; Bhishma knows what is right; the other kings have accepted it.
Then Bhishma speaks, far firmer: someone who won't accept honoring Krishna needn't be coaxed. Both of them tell the truth. Neither one is cruel.
Hinduism has a name for that.
Later in this same epic, in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes kinds of tapas, a word that means heat: the disciplines that train a person.

teach.h: TRUE, KIND, HELPFUL SPEECH IS A TAPAS.
teach.b: One is a discipline of speech: words that don't stir up distress, that are true, pleasant and helpful. That's chapter seventeen. Notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say be soft, or stay silent; many teachers would say Bhishma's firm answer passes too. Shishupala's speech is the one that fails: it isn't kind, and it helps no one.
And through all of it, Krishna hasn't said a word.

how: The Bhagavad Gita (17.15) names a tapas, a discipline, of speech: words that cause no distress, true, pleasant and beneficial, along with regular recitation of scripture. Many Hindus count careful speech as part of spiritual practice, and Yudhishthira's gentleness and Bhishma's firmness in this scene can both be read against it.

o: the elder who says an angry guest needn't be coaxed
the king who argues against Krishna's honor, then walks out
the host who follows an angry guest with gentle words

games.q: one insult, many answers — tap the pairs.
p: argued, insulted, then rose to leave
went after him with gentle words

s: the Gita's discipline of speech means always staying quiet
it asks for words that are true, kind and helpful, so even Bhishma's firm answer can pass.
he went himself and spoke to him gently.
through the objection and the replies, Krishna stayed silent
the host and the elder answer; Krishna hasn't said a word.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. a guest has mocked your choice in front of every king, and now he's walking out. what do you do?
o: go after him and speak gently.
order him removed from the hall.
games.why: Yudhishthira follows him and speaks softly, true words without insult: the tapas of speech, even after being mocked.

practice: Picture a message you've wanted to send someone who stung you. Hold it up to the Gita's tests one at a time: is it true? is it kind? will it help?

Breathe slowly between each one, and let the words change until they pass, or until you see they don't need sending. If you pray, you can offer your words before you speak them; if not, simply rest with the gentler version.

wordCard.voice: Shishupala. The king who argues against Krishna's honor, turns his argument into insult, and walks out, while the host follows him with gentle words.

carryVoice: Your line: true, kind, helpful speech is a tapas. Yudhishthira and Bhishma both passed. That's day seven hundred fifty-nine.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Arghyaharana Parva (Shishupala's objection; Yudhishthira's conciliation; Bhishma's reply)
Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (the tapas, or austerity, of speech)
